A Blender and Unity add-on that helps model developers.
This is a Blender and Unity add-on that helps developers easily
export models to the designated Unity project folder, and also
provides a function to overwrite all objects
using a specific .FBX model with the newly exported .FBX model.
The tool is designed to streamline the workflow between Blender and Unity,
making it more efficient for developers to manage and update their 3D assets.
The application is built using Python for the Blender add-on and C# for the Unity integration.
This tool consists of two main components: a Blender add-on written in Python
and a Unity script written in C#. The Blender add-on allows users to export
their models directly to a specified Unity project folder with a single click.
This was achieved by utilizing Blender's built-in FBX export functionality and
integrating it with a user-friendly interface that allows users to set their
Unity project path and export settings.
One thing that makes this tool stand out is the overwrite function.
This function allows users to overwrite all objects in the Unity project
that use a specific .FBX model with the newly exported .FBX model from Blender.
Designers are often required to make frequent updates to 3D models during the development process.
This function significantly reduces the time and effort needed to update models
in Unity, as users no longer need to manually replace each instance of the model.
Specifically, the overwrite function works by searching through all GameObjects
in the Unity project for references to the old .FBX model and replacing them
with references to the newly exported model.
This is done using Unity's AssetDatabase and GameObject APIs, allowing for
efficient and automated updates to the project.
To facilitate communication between Blender and Unity,
I implemented a UDP connection that allows the two applications to exchange data in real-time.
This connection enables Blender to send export commands to Unity,
and Unity to receive notifications when new models are available.
A json structure is used to format the data being sent over the UDP connection,
ensuring that both applications can easily parse and understand the information.

text: An audio tool automating the looping sound production workflow.
This is a tool developed to help with the sound design and game audio prototyping process.
It now provides several crossfade time options, allowing flexibility when
handling audio assets. 3 modes of crossfade are also available,
each being linear, logarithmic, and sine.
More features are now in development.
The application is built based on Avalonia and the .NET Framework, with the functioning language being C#.
This program emulates the typical way of processing a looping audio in a DAW system.
To make a looping sound, the audio clip will first need to be cut in half and
swapped in position. This means that the former half of the audio now becomes
the latter half, and vice versa. Then, the two audio tracks will need to be overlapped
and crossfaded so they merge perfectly into each other.
This program, essentially, does the same thing.
Using the NAudio library, the program first reads the audio file into a
float array that stores all the data. It then cuts the audio
into two pieces and performs a swapping operation.
The swapped audio data array will then be used to generate the crossfaded
result. The program will start with the midpoint of the array,
perform a special computation (see Phase Issue below),
and mix the two tracks beginning at the computed index.
Different crossfade modes specify how the program will render the
crossfaded area. In its core essence, the program adds the two data
multiplied by a weight coefficient that is calculated
based on the relative index and functions.
After these steps, the audio clip is ready for exporting.
The program will automatically provide a postfix to the
file name if no customized file name is specified.
When dealing with audio, phase is always an issue. This tool has a special computation method,
to the greatest extent, to eliminate the phase problem.
The program, starting at the midpoint of the array, finds the nearest index
at which the wave has an amplitude of zero. This ensures that the
crossfaded audio will always start at a zero point,
avoiding abrupt jumps in phase and amplitude.
A donut making puzzle game made for GMTK 2025.
Dough it Urself is an innovative puzzle game inspired by the GMTK 2025 theme "loop".
While I originally came up with the concept of the game, my teammates collaboratively designed all levels and refined game mechanics.
I worked as a programmer and composer and made the gameplay prototype, some level buildings, and the theme music for this game.
The game is collaboratively done by me, Ruimeng Bai, Enrui Luo, Kexin Liu, Xinran Wei, Hefei Sun.
I started prototyping the game as soon as we settled the basic concept of this game.
The very first version of the game was built using simple geometric shapes, each representing a different game piece.
Using raycasts, I was able to easily detect the exact tile on which the player's cursor
is currently hovering and exclude the obstacles on which no game pieces should be placed.
We confirmed the playability and feasibility of our idea using my prototype, and could thus work more on designing the game.
The win check was one of the difficulties we faced when making the game.
As we have designed, a legal "donut" is a closed loop of a uniform 1 width,
and at least 1 empty tile must be enveloped by such a loop.
To convert this into a solvable programming problem, I concluded that,
within such a legal shape, each piece (dough block) must have exactly 2 adjacent blocks.
This ensures that the shape would have a uniform width of 1 unit,
and it prevents two blocks from connecting diagonally.
This, however, does not ensure that the shape envelops at least 1 empty tile. To solve this issue,
I randomly pick one dough block as the origin, and send a ray to every other dough block.
As long as the ray hits one empty tile, the shape is legal.
This would not cause any issue even if the hit empty tile is not enclosed by the loop,
because we have previously checked that the blocks that make up the shape have and only
have 2 adjacent blocks, where no solid convex shape would be identified as legal.
When selecting levels, the camera moves as the cursor is near both the left and right edges of the screen.
This is achieved by constantly comparing the mouse's position and the threshold, which is computed by:
Threshold Position = Screen Width x Ratio
The camera movement is locked when the camera hits a "stopper", placed on both sides of the screen.
This prevents the camera from moving too far.
The level selection button effect is made possible by changing material colors.
To detect any possible clicking and hovering, we send out a ray to see if the cursor is hovering above a button.
If it does, the material of that particular button is darkened to mimic a highlight effect.
This is, in fact, how most of our buttons work in the game.
The level selection buttons are all connected to an individual level,
which the player goes to when pressing the buttons.

Over the 3-month development duration, we crafted this nature-themed 2.5D platformer game.
I worked primarily on designing the game, composing music, and implementing the audio,
as well as building levels and recording cutscene videos.
The game is collaboratively created by me, Kai Dodson, Chenyen Liaw, and Evan Beck.
In the early stage of designing, we brainstormed the basic structure of our game,
including the essential characters, plots, and other important elements.
We set up deadlines for solidifying our story, game mechanics, and art.
As we approached the end of pre-production, we started designing levels.
We had our initial version drafted on paper,
and the finalized one in Figma, where we collectively contributed.
Later in Unity, we were each responsible for building one section of the game scene,
where we put every section together after we finished. We were also making slight changes
while we were building the levels, in order to avoid any unreasonable setup,

I integrated and implemented all audio in the game using the audio middleware Wwise.
All audio preparation work was done in Logic Pro.
The sounds I utilized are either from copyright-free sources or those that I recorded.
By using Wwise, I was able to have better control over the triggering and pausing of each audio event.
Three soundbanks were used, each controlling ambience, sound effects, and music.
Interactive music is made possible through the use of Wwise.
The game features multiple areas that the player can explore as they progress in the game.
As we have designed, the music changes,
without being paused or having any abrupt gaps, when the player enters each area.
To achieve this, the music is bounced into individual clips while also separated into stems.
As is shown in the picture, MUS_State_1 has only the Keys layer, whereas MUS_State_6 has all six layers:
bass, bells, drum kit, keys, and lead. All these layers are different from each other,
which creates the desired change from one section to another.
Each music section is bound to a Wwise state, which is triggered and manipulated in
Unity as the player enters each trigger zone.
The state then tells Wwise to change the music,
based on what is set when designed.
I used RTPC as a method to control the game volume and present certain effects.
To control volume, there is a slider in the settings page,
which is connected to the RTPC parameter in Wwise.
This RTPC controls the output volume of the master bus
of the whole game audio system,
where every sound is subject to change.
Another RTPC is used to change the volume of the vine swing.
This RTPC is linked to the player's velocity,
and the greater the player's velocity is,
the louder the sound effect is.
I also created different footstep sounds,
and they are played randomly as the player moves.
Specifically, the footsteps sound is crafted so that
they sound different when the player is stepping on dirt and grass.
A Wwise switch container is used, and the particular switch is
triggered by a raycast shot vertically down from the player to the ground,
detecting the material of the ground block.
The footsteps, specifically, are triggered through animation events,
which are broadcast each time the player model's feet touch the ground.
the audio is always in sync with the visual to avoid a discrepancy.

Sisyphus's Worst Day is a USC Advanced Game Project developed over 10 months.
It is a third-person puzzle game that reimagines the myth of Sisyphus in a humorous, modern setting.
Players take on the role of an office worker guided by the gods, who must trap Sisyphus in an endless loop of mundane tasks.
As the Lead Technical Sound Designer, I oversaw the audio production process and ensured that every sound element was effectively integrated into the game through FMOD and Unity.
I collaborated closely with four other sound designers to create an immersive audio experience that complemented the game's distinctive narrative and gameplay mechanics.
The audio implementation process involved using FMOD to create interactive audio events and Unity to integrate these events into the game.
I developed a structured workflow that allowed for efficient collaboration between the sound design team and the development team,
ensuring that all audio assets were properly organized and implemented.
The FMOD project was managed and maintained in Perforce, allowing for version control and collaboration among fellow sound designers.
We organized and categorized all audio assets in FMOD, ensuring a consistent and efficient workflow.
The game featureed an interactive music system that dynamically changes music based on the state of the game.
There were 2 stages in the game, both placing stage (where the player sets up the puzzle) and playing stage (where Sisyphus attempts to push the boulder).
The music would do a horizontal change, meaning the two fully mixed tracks would crossfade when the transition happens. This was achieved by using FMOD's parameter system.
All diegetic sound effects were implemented in 3D space using FMOD's 3D audio capabilities. This allowed for a more immersive experience,

The ScriptableObjects automtically linked the voiceover lines to their respective audio files, ensuring that the game system would get the correct audio file for each line of dialogue.
To manage each voice data, we also created a VoiceOver ScriptableObject that contained a list of all the voice lines for a specific character or scene.
This allowed us to easily organize and manage the voiceover content, making it easier to implement and maintain throughout the development process.

A standalone WAAPI tool for browsing, previewing, and controlling Wwise sound objects without leaving a designer-focused interface.
The main workspace after loading a Wwise project

SoundBoard began with a simple workflow problem: designers often need to audition sounds and test interactive parameters, but opening an engine integration or moving through several Wwise views adds friction to a quick creative decision.

I designed a standalone desktop tool that connects directly to an open Wwise project through the Wwise Authoring API. It collects the project hierarchy and presents the controls attached to each sound object in one place, so events can be previewed and RTPC or Switch values can be tested in real time without relying on Unity.
The goal was not to replace Wwise. It was to create a focused layer on top of it—one that makes the parts most useful during sound review immediately visible and playable.

SoundBoard opens with a small connection wizard. Once a Wwise project is open and WAAPI is enabled in its project settings, the tool establishes the connection and loads the available sound objects automatically.

Keeping this step separate from the main window makes the application state clear: the user knows whether Wwise is ready before any project controls appear, while connection and data-loading errors remain contained in a simple entry point.

The left panel turns the connected Wwise project into a collapsible tree. Folders, Switch Containers, and regular sound objects use distinct visual markers, allowing the structure to stay readable even in a larger project.

I also added keyword search and an option to hide the Factory folders included with Wwise 2025. Both filters work from a preserved copy of the complete hierarchy, so users can change search terms or restore hidden content without querying Wwise again or losing the original structure.
All controls associated with the selected sound object

Selecting a sound object opens a detail panel with its Wwise notes, related Events, RTPCs, and Switch Groups. Event names are retrieved directly from the project, and each play button posts the corresponding event to the Wwise Sound Engine.

RTPC ranges are read from their curves and displayed as sliders, with both drag control and direct numeric entry. Slider changes are lightly debounced before being sent through WAAPI, keeping the response immediate without flooding Wwise with redundant updates. Switch options are also loaded automatically and can be changed from a dropdown.
Bringing these relationships into one view helps designers hear what an object does and understand what drives it at the same time.

I defined the product direction, supervised the overall architecture, and made the high-level structural adjustments throughout development. An AI agent handled the concrete implementation of the Avalonia interface and MVVM structure under that direction.

I implemented the Wwise Authoring API integration myself, including project queries, event playback, RTPC control, Switch changes, and the connection workflow. Keeping WAAPI communication behind dedicated services allowed the generated interface layer and the Wwise-facing logic to evolve without becoming tightly coupled.

Because the Wwise project may keep changing while SoundBoard is open, Refresh Project rebuilds the object hierarchy and control data on demand. Newly added Events, RTPCs, and Switch Groups can enter the same workflow without restarting the application.

text: Jianghao Li - Unity Audio Callback System
An open-source, thread-safe callback workflow for synchronizing Unity events with precise moments in audio.

Unity's built-in audio system can play clips reliably, but synchronizing gameplay, animation, or visual effects to exact moments in those clips often requires one-off timing code. I built this system to bring a marker-and-callback workflow—similar to the event callbacks found in FMOD and Wwise—directly into a standard Unity project.
Designers package a clip, playback settings, and named markers inside an

then plays the clip and invokes each marker's UnityEvent at the correct moment. The same marker can also be found by name from code, making the workflow useful both in the Inspector and through runtime subscriptions.
The result is a lightweight, open-source layer that keeps audio timing reusable, visible, and close to the people authoring the experience.
is the system's source of truth. Alongside the AudioClip, it stores volume, pitch, looping, spatial blend, mixer routing, and whether callbacks should retrigger on each loop.

Each marker combines a readable name, a timestamp, and a UnityEvent. This separates the timing data from any one scene object, so the same authored audio event can be assigned to different players and wired to different gameplay responses.

and only then invokes each marker's UnityEvent. The queue forms a clear thread boundary: the audio thread owns precise timing detection, while the main thread owns every Unity-facing side effect. No shared list is iterated by both threads, and no lock is held inside the real-time audio callback.
Looping clips can optionally reset the marker index and retrigger their events on every pass, while one-shot playback naturally stops processing once the clip ends.

I created a custom Unity Editor window so timing can be authored by listening and looking, instead of repeatedly entering seconds by hand. It renders the selected clip's waveform, previews audio with a moving cursor, and provides zoom and horizontal navigation for precise placement.

Markers can be added directly on the waveform, dragged to a new moment, selected from the list, renamed, deleted, or fine-tuned numerically. The selected marker's UnityEvent is exposed in the same window, keeping timing and behavior together throughout iteration.

This keeps cinematic and gameplay workflows on the same reusable AudioEventAsset model instead of requiring a second timing implementation.
An innovative 3D adventure game that talks about alienation and self-discovery.
This game received the Best Art Design Award at the 2026 Global Game Jam.
Whiteout is an innovative 3D adventure game that explores themes of alienation and self-discovery.
The game is completed in 48 hours as part of a game jam event.
We aimed to create an immersive experience where players navigate through a surreal environment,
solving puzzles and uncovering the protagonist's story.
We focused on atmospheric design, combining visual aesthetics with a haunting soundtrack to enhance the emotional impact.
I designed the core gameplay mechanics, implemented such simulations, and composed the game's soundtrack to complement the narrative.
The game was collaboratively developed with Aerina Fu, Dayuan Dong, Yuxiang Wang, and Kairui Xu.
The game was developed for a 48 hour game jam, whose theme was "Mask".
We brainstormed various ideas and finally settled on the idea where we
interpret "Mask" both as an emotional mask that people wear to hide their true selves, and
as a way to shield oneself from the harsh realities of the world.
I led the conversation and the brainstorming session, and proposed the idea of an adventure game
where the player explores a surreal world while uncovering the protagonist's story.
We thus decided that our experience goal was to make player feel isolated but cured in the end.
To achieve the feeling of isolation and alienation, we designed the core mechanics of the game,
one of which was that the player needs to avoid light sources in the environment, as they represent societal pressures
that the protagonist is trying to escape from.
We also designed a unique mechanic where the player can throw ink to create a temporary shield against light,
symbolizing the emotional masks people wear.
One of the main mechanics of the game is to avoid light sources.
While there were many ways to implement this, one of which we considered was to use shader
programming to check the brightness of the pixel where the player is located, we thought that
it would be too challenging to implement within the time constraint of a 48-hour game jam.
Instead, I proposed a simpler yet effective method to achieve this.
By design, the game has only one directional light source in any given scene, which made the implementation
much easier. I set up a system that constantly sends out a ray from the light source's position to that of the player,
and check if the ray hits any obstacle before reaching the player.
The light manager singleton handles all light sources in the scene.
In the Update function, it iterates through all light sources and performs their respective execution logic.
If the execution logic returns true, it means that the player is exposed to that light source,
and light manager will invoke an event to notify other systems, such as the player handler to hanle the consequences.
On the other hand, if no light source exposes the player, another event is invoked to notify that the player is safe.
Although in the current version of the game, there is only one light source,
we specifically designed the light system to be easily extendable to support multiple light sources in the future.
To achieve this, we created a base class for light sources, which serves a common interface.
All light sources inherit from this base class and implement their own execution logic if needed.
As is shown in the code snippet, the base class provides a virtual Execute method, which allows
derived classes to override it with their specific logic.
Another core and innovative mechanic of the game is the ink throwing mechanic, where the player can throw ink to create a temporary shield against light.
This mechanic is designed to symbolize the emotional masks people wear to protect themselves from societal pressures.
As we designed, the player could pick up ink from certain locations in the environment. By throwing the ink, the player
creates a splash of ink at the target location, which serves as a safe zone that will prevents
the player from being exposed to light sources when they are within the ink area.
We used the decal system in Unity to create the ink splash effect. When the player throws ink, a decal is instantiated at the target location, which creates a circular area that blocks light.
The decal will render on top of the environment and characters, creating a visually distinct safe zone for the player.
A trigger collider zone is set up so that when the player enters, stays, or exits the ink area, the light manager will be notified to update the player's exposure status accordingly.
To enhance the gameplay experience of the ink throwing mechanic, we implemented a trajectory prediction system to help players aim their throws more accurately.
When the player is aiming the throw, a trajectory line is rendered from the player's position to the target location, showing the predicted path of the ink splash.
We created a static class for trajectory calculation, which uses physics equations to calculate the trajectory points based on the initial velocity and gravity.

text: An audio tool automating the looping sound production workflow.
This is a tool developed to help with the sound design and game audio prototyping process.
It now provides several crossfade time options, allowing flexibility when
handling audio assets. 3 modes of crossfade are also available,
each being linear, logarithmic, and sine.
More features are now in development.
The application is built based on Avalonia and the .NET Framework, with the functioning language being C#.
This program emulates the typical way of processing a looping audio in a DAW system.
To make a looping sound, the audio clip will first need to be cut in half and
swapped in position. This means that the former half of the audio now becomes
the latter half, and vice versa. Then, the two audio tracks will need to be overlapped
and crossfaded so they merge perfectly into each other.
This program, essentially, does the same thing.
Using the NAudio library, the program first reads the audio file into a
float array that stores all the data. It then cuts the audio
into two pieces and performs a swapping operation.
The swapped audio data array will then be used to generate the crossfaded
result. The program will start with the midpoint of the array,
perform a special computation (see Phase Issue below),
and mix the two tracks beginning at the computed index.
Different crossfade modes specify how the program will render the
crossfaded area. In its core essence, the program adds the two data
multiplied by a weight coefficient that is calculated
based on the relative index and functions.
After these steps, the audio clip is ready for exporting.
The program will automatically provide a postfix to the
file name if no customized file name is specified.
When dealing with audio, phase is always an issue. This tool has a special computation method,
to the greatest extent, to eliminate the phase problem.
The program, starting at the midpoint of the array, finds the nearest index
at which the wave has an amplitude of zero. This ensures that the
crossfaded audio will always start at a zero point,
avoiding abrupt jumps in phase and amplitude.

The game is collaboratively done by me, Ruimeng Bai, Enrui Luo, Kexin Liu, Xinran Wei, Hefei Sun.
I started prototyping the game as soon as we settled the basic concept of this game.
The very first version of the game was built using simple geometric shapes, each representing a different game piece.
Using raycasts, I was able to easily detect the exact tile on which the player's cursor
is currently hovering and exclude the obstacles on which no game pieces should be placed.
We confirmed the playability and feasibility of our idea using my prototype, and could thus work more on designing the game.
The win check was one of the difficulties we faced when making the game.
As we have designed, a legal "donut" is a closed loop of a uniform 1 width,
and at least 1 empty tile must be enveloped by such a loop.
To convert this into a solvable programming problem, I concluded that,
within such a legal shape, each piece (dough block) must have exactly 2 adjacent blocks.
This ensures that the shape would have a uniform width of 1 unit,
and it prevents two blocks from connecting diagonally.
This, however, does not ensure that the shape envelops at least 1 empty tile. To solve this issue,
I randomly pick one dough block as the origin, and send a ray to every other dough block.
As long as the ray hits one empty tile, the shape is legal.
This would not cause any issue even if the hit empty tile is not enclosed by the loop,
because we have previously checked that the blocks that make up the shape have and only
have 2 adjacent blocks, where no solid convex shape would be identified as legal.
When selecting levels, the camera moves as the cursor is near both the left and right edges of the screen.
This is achieved by constantly comparing the mouse's position and the threshold, which is computed by:
Threshold Position = Screen Width x Ratio
The camera movement is locked when the camera hits a "stopper", placed on both sides of the screen.
This prevents the camera from moving too far.
The level selection button effect is made possible by changing material colors.
To detect any possible clicking and hovering, we send out a ray to see if the cursor is hovering above a button.
If it does, the material of that particular button is darkened to mimic a highlight effect.
This is, in fact, how most of our buttons work in the game.
The level selection buttons are all connected to an individual level,
which the player goes to when pressing the buttons.

This RTPC controls the output volume of the master bus

An innovative 3D adventure game that talks about alienation and self-discovery.

Whiteout is an innovative 3D adventure game that explores themes of alienation and self-discovery.
The game is completed in 48 hours as part of a game jam event.
We aimed to create an immersive experience where players navigate through a surreal environment,
solving puzzles and uncovering the protagonist's story.
We focused on atmospheric design, combining visual aesthetics with a haunting soundtrack to enhance the emotional impact.
I designed the core gameplay mechanics, implemented such simulations, and composed the game's soundtrack to complement the narrative.
The game was collaboratively developed with Aerina Fu, Dayuan Dong, Yuxiang Wang, and Kairui Xu.
The game was developed for a 48 hour game jam, whose theme was "Mask".
We brainstormed various ideas and finally settled on the idea where we
interpret "Mask" both as an emotional mask that people wear to hide their true selves, and
as a way to shield oneself from the harsh realities of the world.
I led the conversation and the brainstorming session, and proposed the idea of an adventure game
where the player explores a surreal world while uncovering the protagonist's story.
We thus decided that our experience goal was to make player feel isolated but cured in the end.
To achieve the feeling of isolation and alienation, we designed the core mechanics of the game,
one of which was that the player needs to avoid light sources in the environment, as they represent societal pressures
that the protagonist is trying to escape from.
We also designed a unique mechanic where the player can throw ink to create a temporary shield against light,
symbolizing the emotional masks people wear.
One of the main mechanics of the game is to avoid light sources.
While there were many ways to implement this, one of which we considered was to use shader
programming to check the brightness of the pixel where the player is located, we thought that
it would be too challenging to implement within the time constraint of a 48-hour game jam.
Instead, I proposed a simpler yet effective method to achieve this.
By design, the game has only one directional light source in any given scene, which made the implementation
much easier. I set up a system that constantly sends out a ray from the light source's position to that of the player,
and check if the ray hits any obstacle before reaching the player.
The light manager singleton handles all light sources in the scene.
In the Update function, it iterates through all light sources and performs their respective execution logic.
If the execution logic returns true, it means that the player is exposed to that light source,
and light manager will invoke an event to notify other systems, such as the player handler to hanle the consequences.
On the other hand, if no light source exposes the player, another event is invoked to notify that the player is safe.
Although in the current version of the game, there is only one light source,
we specifically designed the light system to be easily extendable to support multiple light sources in the future.
To achieve this, we created a base class for light sources, which serves a common interface.
All light sources inherit from this base class and implement their own execution logic if needed.
As is shown in the code snippet, the base class provides a virtual Execute method, which allows
derived classes to override it with their specific logic.
Another core and innovative mechanic of the game is the ink throwing mechanic, where the player can throw ink to create a temporary shield against light.
This mechanic is designed to symbolize the emotional masks people wear to protect themselves from societal pressures.
As we designed, the player could pick up ink from certain locations in the environment. By throwing the ink, the player
creates a splash of ink at the target location, which serves as a safe zone that will prevents
the player from being exposed to light sources when they are within the ink area.
We used the decal system in Unity to create the ink splash effect. When the player throws ink, a decal is instantiated at the target location, which creates a circular area that blocks light.
The decal will render on top of the environment and characters, creating a visually distinct safe zone for the player.
A trigger collider zone is set up so that when the player enters, stays, or exits the ink area, the light manager will be notified to update the player's exposure status accordingly.
To enhance the gameplay experience of the ink throwing mechanic, we implemented a trajectory prediction system to help players aim their throws more accurately.
When the player is aiming the throw, a trajectory line is rendered from the player's position to the target location, showing the predicted path of the ink splash.
We created a static class for trajectory calculation, which uses physics equations to calculate the trajectory points based on the initial velocity and gravity.
The trajectory line is updated in real-time as the player adjusts their aim, providing immediate feedback on where the ink will land.

为了制作循环声音，音频剪辑首先需要被切成两半并交换位置。
这意味着音频的前半部分现在成为后半部分，反之亦然。然后，这两条音频轨道需要重叠
并进行交叉淡化，以使它们完美地融合在一起。
该程序本质上做了同样的事情。
使用 NAudio 库，程序首先将音频文件读取到一个存储所有数据的浮点数组中。然后将音频切成两部分并执行交换操作。
交换后的音频数据数组将用于生成交叉淡化的结果。程序将从数组的中点开始，

胜利判定是我们在制作游戏时面临的难题之一。
正如我们设计的那样，一个合法的“甜甜圈”是一个宽度均匀为1的闭合环路，

为了将其转化为一个可解决的编程问题，我得出结论，在这样一个合法的形状中，每个块（面团块）必须恰好有2个相邻的块。
这确保了形状的宽度为1个单位的均匀宽度，

然而，这并不能确保形状包围了至少1个空格。为了解决这个问题，
我随机选择一个面团块作为起点，并向每个其他面团块发送一条射线。
只要射线击中一个空格，形状就是合法的。
即使被击中的空格没有被环路包围，这也不会导致任何问题，
因为我们之前已经检查过组成形状的块恰好有2个相邻的块，
这样就不会将任何实心凸形状识别为合法形状。

阈值位置 = 屏幕宽度 x 比例

一款通过 WAAPI 独立运行的 Wwise 音频工具，让设计师能够在更专注的界面中浏览、试听并控制声音对象。
载入 Wwise 项目后的主工作界面
SoundBoard 起源于一个很实际的工作流问题：设计师经常需要快速试听声音、测试交互参数，但如果每次都要打开游戏引擎集成，或在 Wwise 的多个界面之间来回切换，一次简单的创作判断也会被打断。
因此，我设计了这款能够通过 Wwise Authoring API 直接连接已打开项目的独立桌面工具。它会读取项目层级，并把每个声音对象所关联的控制集中展示出来。设计师不必依赖 Unity，就能实时试听 Event、调整 RTPC，或切换 Switch 状态。
我的目标并不是取代 Wwise，而是在它之上增加一层更专注的入口，让声音审阅时最常用的信息和操作能够立即被看到、被听到。
SoundBoard 启动时会先显示一个简洁的连接向导。只要 Wwise 项目已经打开，并在项目设置中启用了 WAAPI，工具就会建立连接并自动读取可用的声音对象。
我将连接步骤与主窗口分开，让应用当前所处的状态更清楚：在任何项目控制出现之前，用户能够先确认 Wwise 是否准备就绪；连接与数据载入的问题，也会被限制在一个简单明确的入口中。
左侧面板会把连接到的 Wwise 项目转换为可展开的树状结构。文件夹、Switch Container 和普通声音对象拥有不同的视觉标记，即使项目规模变大，层级关系依然容易辨认。
我还加入了关键词搜索，以及隐藏 Wwise 2025 Factory 默认文件夹的选项。两种筛选都会从完整层级的保留副本中生成结果，因此用户可以随时更换搜索内容或恢复被隐藏的对象，无须重新向 Wwise 请求数据，也不会破坏原有结构。
集中显示所选声音对象的全部关联控制
让控制回到声音语境中
选择一个声音对象后，右侧详情面板会显示它在 Wwise 中的备注，以及相关的 Event、RTPC 和 Switch Group。Event 名称直接从项目中获取，每个播放按钮都会把对应事件发送给 Wwise Sound Engine。
RTPC 的范围会从曲线中自动读取，并转换成滑杆；用户既可以拖动控制，也可以直接输入数值。滑动产生的变化会经过轻量节流后再通过 WAAPI 发送，在维持即时反馈的同时，避免向 Wwise 提交过多重复更新。Switch 选项同样会被自动读取，并通过下拉菜单切换。
当这些关系被放在同一个界面里，设计师可以一边听见声音对象的实际表现，一边理解究竟有哪些参数正在驱动它。
我负责定义产品方向、监督整体架构，并在开发过程中进行宏观层面的结构调整。在这一方向下，Avalonia 界面与 MVVM 架构的具体代码实现由 AI agent 完成。
Wwise Authoring API 的集成则由我独立完成，包括项目数据查询、Event 播放、RTPC 控制、Switch 切换和连接流程。将 WAAPI 通信放在独立的服务层中，也让 AI 实现的界面层与面向 Wwise 的核心逻辑可以分别迭代，而不会彼此紧密耦合。
考虑到设计师可能会在 SoundBoard 开启期间继续修改 Wwise 项目，我加入了 Refresh Project 功能，按需重新构建对象层级和控制数据。新增的 Event、RTPC 与 Switch Group 因此能够直接进入同一套工作流，无须重启应用。

text: Jianghao Li - Unity 音频回调系统
一套开源、线程安全的回调工作流，用于将 Unity 事件与音频中的精确时间点同步。
Unity 内置音频系统能够稳定地播放音频，但若要让游戏逻辑、动画或视觉效果与音频中的精确时刻同步，往往需要为每个场景单独编写计时代码。我开发了这套系统，将 FMOD 和 Wwise 中常见的“标记 + 回调”工作流直接带入标准 Unity 项目。
中统一保存音频片段、播放参数和具名标记。
负责播放音频，并在准确时刻触发每个标记对应的 UnityEvent；其他脚本也可以通过名称查找并订阅回调，因此该系统同时支持 Inspector 配置和运行时代码两种使用方式。
最终成果是一套轻量、开源的音频事件层，让时间信息可以复用、可视化，并始终贴近内容创作者的工作流程。
可复用的音频事件资产
是系统的数据核心。除了 AudioClip，它还保存音量、音高、循环、空间混合、Mixer 路由，以及循环时是否重复触发回调等参数。
每个标记由易读名称、时间戳和 UnityEvent 组成。计时数据因此不再依附于某个场景对象，同一份音频事件资产可以被不同播放器复用，并连接到不同的游戏反馈。
单个标记的时间与回调数据
对照波形试听并检查标记时间
线程安全是系统设计的核心
中检查已经过的 DSP 时间。由于该回调运行在 Unity 音频线程，系统绝不会在这里直接触发 UnityEvent 或访问游戏对象；到达时间点的标记只会通过非阻塞的
，并在成功取出标记后才触发对应的 UnityEvent。这条队列建立了清晰的线程边界：音频线程只负责精确的时间检测，主线程负责所有与 Unity 对象相关的副作用。两个线程不会同时遍历同一个共享列表，实时音频回调中也不需要持有锁。
对于循环音频，设计师可以选择在每次循环时重置标记索引并再次触发事件；非循环音频则会在播放结束后自然停止处理。
一条队列，两种清晰的线程职责
音频线程：检测标记时间，只负责入队
主线程：取出标记，安全触发 UnityEvent
我制作了自定义 Unity Editor 窗口，让设计师可以通过聆听和观察来调整时间，而不是反复手动输入秒数。编辑器会绘制当前音频的波形，支持带移动指针的音频预览，并提供缩放与水平滚动，以便进行精细定位。
用户可以直接点击波形添加标记、拖拽调整时间、从列表中选中、重命名、删除或输入精确数值。所选标记的 UnityEvent 也在同一窗口中编辑，让时间和行为在迭代过程中始终保持在一起。
直接在波形上添加和拖拽标记

、PlayableAsset 和 PlayableBehaviour 将同一事件系统扩展到 Unity Timeline。AudioEventPlayer 可以绑定到轨道，让播放与回调跟随 Timeline Graph，与动画、粒子、镜头及其他序列内容共同运行。
电影化内容与常规游戏逻辑因此可以复用同一套 AudioEventAsset 数据模型，无需维护第二套计时实现。

Whiteout 是一款创新的 3D 冒险游戏，探索疏离和自我发现的主题。
该游戏在 48 小时内完成，作为一次游戏开发竞赛的一部分。
我们旨在创造一种沉浸式体验，让玩家在超现实的环境中导航，
解决谜题并揭示主角的故事。
我们专注于氛围设计，将视觉美学与令人难忘的配乐相结合，以增强情感影响。
我设计了核心游戏机制，实现了相关模拟，并为游戏配乐以补充叙事。
该游戏由 Aerina Fu、Dayuan Dong、Yuxiang Wang 和 Kairui Xu 共同开发。
该游戏是在一个为期48小时的游戏开发竞赛中开发的，主题是“面具”。
我们头脑风暴了各种想法，最终确定了一个既将“面具”解释为人们用来隐藏真实自我的情感面具，
又作为一种保护自己免受世界严酷现实伤害的方式的想法。
我领导了讨论和头脑风暴会议，提出了一个冒险游戏的想法，
玩家在探索超现实世界的同时揭示主角的故事。
因此，我们决定我们的体验目标是让玩家感到孤立，但最终得到治愈。
为了实现孤立和疏离的感觉，我们设计了游戏的核心机制，
其中之一是玩家需要避免环境中的光源，因为它们代表了主角试图逃避的社会压力。
我们还设计了一个独特的机制，玩家可以投掷墨水以创建一个临时的光盾，
象征着人们戴着的情感面具。
游戏的主要机制之一是避免光源。
虽然有许多实现方法，其中一种是使用着色器编程来检查玩家所在像素的亮度，但我们认为在48小时的游戏开发竞赛时间限制内实现这一点太具挑战性。
相反，我提出了一种更简单但有效的方法来实现这一点。
由于设计上，游戏在任何给定场景中只有一个方向光源，这使得实现变得
更加容易。我设置了一个系统，不断地从光源的位置向玩家的位置发送射线，
并检查射线在到达玩家之前是否击中了任何障碍物。
Light Manager 是一个单例类，负责管理场景中的所有光源。在 Update 函数中，它会遍历所有光源并执行它们各自的执行逻辑。
如果执行逻辑返回 true，意味着玩家暴露在那个光源下，光线管理器将调用一个事件来通知其他系统，例如玩家处理器来处理后果。
反之，如果没有光源照在玩家身上，则会调用另一个事件以广播玩家目前安全的状态。
虽然在当前版本的游戏中只有一个光源，
我们特别设计了光源系统，使其易于扩展以支持未来的多个光源。
为此，我们创建了一个光源基类，作为一个通用接口。
所有光源都继承自这个基类，并根据需要实现自己的执行逻辑。
如代码片段所示，基类提供了一个虚拟的 Execute 方法，允许派生类用它们的特定逻辑来重写该方法。
派生类可以用它们的特定逻辑来重写该方法。
玩家在墨水溅射上创建安全区
游戏的另一个核心且创新的机制是墨水投掷机制，玩家可以投掷墨水以创建一个临时的光线屏障。
这个机制旨在象征人们为了保护自己免受社会压力而戴上的情感面具。
正如我们设计的那样，玩家可以从环境中的特定位置拾取墨水。通过投掷墨水，玩家
会在目标位置创建一个墨水溅射区域，该区域作为一个安全区，当玩家处于墨水区域内时，可以防止
我们使用 Unity 中的贴花系统来创建墨水溅射效果。当玩家投掷墨水时，在目标位置实例化一个贴花，创建一个圆形区域来阻挡光线。
贴花会渲染在环境和角色的上方，为玩家创建一个视觉上明显的安全区。
设置了一个触发器碰撞器区域，当玩家进入、停留或离开墨水区域时，光源管理器会收到通知，从而相应地更新玩家的暴露状态。
为了增强墨水投掷机制的游戏体验，我们实现了一个轨迹预测系统，帮助玩家更准确地瞄准投掷目标。
当玩家瞄准投掷时，会从玩家的位置到目标位置渲染一条轨迹线，显示墨水溅射的预测路径。
我们创建了一个用于轨迹计算的静态类，该类使用物理方程根据初始速度和重力计算轨迹点。
随着玩家调整瞄准，轨迹线会实时更新，提供墨水落点的即时反馈。
